title: Functional Multiple-Spine Calcium Imaging from Brain Slices
protocol: Prepare artificial cerebrospinal fluid (aCSF).
Prepare patch-clamp pipettes.
Prepare standard pipettes with resistance of 4–6 MΩ for somatic recordings.
Dissolve a 20 μl aliquot of 1 mM stock solution of Fluo-4 pentapotassium salt in intracellular solution to a final concentration of 200 μM.
Keep the dissolved Fluo-4 solution on ice throughout the experiment.
Cut the membrane around a slice using a surgical microknife and transfer the slice to a recording chamber perfused with aCSF warmed to 32–34°C.
Perfuse the slice with 200 μM Trolox in aCSF to reduce phototoxicity and photobleaching.
Maintain the speed of aCSF perfusion at 2–4 mL/min.
Place a platinum anchor on the slice membrane to keep it from being dislodged by the perfusion solution.
Trim the membrane to leave enough room for the platinum anchor.
Stabilize the slice in the recording chamber for 15 minutes to reduce movement during recording.
Search and focus on a healthy neuron using a 60× objective lens.
Use differential interference contrast or gradient contrast video microscope if necessary to facilitate patch-clamping.
Load dendrites with a calcium indicator by performing whole-cell recording from the soma.
Prepare intracellular solution containing 200 μM Fluo-4 (or Fluo-5F).
Use a glass pipette with resistance of 4–6 MΩ.
Position the pipette tip carefully at the selected soma with positive pressure of 50–100 kN/m².
Release pipette pressure and apply gentle suction (∼20 kN/m²) to establish whole-cell configuration.
Assess patch configuration by applying repetitive 10-mV test pulses using a patch-clamp amplifier.
Wait until dendrites are sufficiently labeled with the calcium indicator, approximately 10 minutes for pyramidal cells.
Adjust parameters of image acquisition to avoid phototoxicity and photobleaching.
Set frame rates between 100–333 Hz for optimal results.
Set spinning-disk rotation speeds between 5,000–10,000 rotations per minute (rpm).
Ensure cells are not exposed to light to prevent phototoxicity.
Switch to the voltage-clamp mode for current recording.
Set the holding voltage at −30 mV.
Find an appropriate region of the dendritic field of the patched neuron.
Place the selected region in the center of the field of view.
Minimize the space-clamp effect by imaging only spines within 200 μm of the soma.
Use laser power less than 1 mW to prevent photodamage.
Adjust laser intensities for optimal signal-to-noise ratio.
Start image acquisition for the duration required by the experiment.
Reduce interference fringes by adjusting the rotational speed of the Nipkow disk or the video rate if necessary.
Record EPSCs or IPSCs simultaneously with spine activity using a TTL trigger to synchronize imaging and electrophysiology recording.
Acquire a z-stack of images of the dendritic branches for post hoc three-dimensional reconstruction of the recorded spines (frame rate: 1 frame/s).
Determine the regions of interest (ROIs) that encompass the recorded spines based on the coordinate of the center of a given spine and the radius of the spine.
Average the fluorescence intensities of all pixels within each ROI for each frame and generate a time series of the mean fluorescence for individual spines.
Apply the modified Okada filter to the time series of mean fluorescence.
Compare the fluorescence intensity xt at time t with preceding and following values xt–1 and xt+1.
If xt is the median among xt–1, xt, and xt+1, do not change xt.
If xt is not the median, replace xt with (xt–1 + Zxt + xt+1)/(2 + Z).
Calculate coefficient Z as (xt+1 – M)/SD, where M and SD are calculated from the entire time series {xt}.
Plot the substituted value (xt–1 + Zxt + xt+1)/(2 + Z) as a function of Z.
When Z is 0, replace xt with the mean of xt–1 and xt+1, i.e., (xt–1 + xt+1)/2.
As Z increases, make (xt–1 + Zxt + xt+1)/(2 + Z) closer to xt.
If noise remains in the processed data, reapply the modified Okada filter.
Extract signals from calcium fluctuations.
Determine the timing of spine activity manually or automatically based on the onsets of calcium transients.
